2.text: Not all the Chukchee are of this irascible type. Some are quiet and

3.text: good-natured, often prone to loquaciousness and to giving reasons even for

4.text: obvious things; but these also are not free from occasional outbursts of anger.

5.text: An old man named Aiñanwaˊt, who had lived with me for two years in the

6.text: Kolyma country, and had patiently helped me the whole time even in the

7.text: most tedious ethnographical work, told me an incident of his former life.

8.text: When vexed by the unruliness of his reindeer-herd, he so lost his patience

9.text: that he suddenly stopped running after the reindeer, and, turning to the setting

10.text: sun, invited the wolves to come and devour the herd. According to the

11.text: belief of the Reindeer Chukchee, such words amount almost to a sacrilege;

12.text: since the wolves are classed with evil spirits, and the curse, once uttered aloud,

13.text: can never be revoked, because it becomes a promise of sacrifice. Within a

14.text: few moments the exasperated herdsman realized what he had done, and tried

15.text: to avoid the disastrous consequences by the sacrifice of his best team, but it

16.text: was of no avail. His luck had turned, and his herd suffered misfortune

18.text: In addition to this irritability, the Chukchee shows a peculiar obstinacy

19.text: in accomplishing whatever seems of momentary interest to him. In trading,

20.text: when a Chukchee has set his heart on any trifling object, he is often ready

21.text: to offer thrice, or even ten times, the price of it. If his offer is not accepted,

22.text: he will start a brawl rather than desist from his purpose of his own free will.

23.text: The small Russian traders sometimes skilfully avail themselves of this weakness

24.text: by goading their wild customers on, and then withholding the article, in order

25.text: to get a larger price for it. In a wrestling-match the defeated competitor

26.text: will again and again try his luck, though repeatedly thrown, until at last a

27.text: fight ensues. When thwarted in his purpose, the Chukchee is ready to go

28.text: to any extreme, even to committing suicide, from uncontrollable rage. I know

29.text: an instance of a young girl who went out to the herd and hung herself to a
29.note: First word 'an' has damaged/inked type (n's foot flourish reads like 'rf' at 2x), confirmed as 'an' by context and letterform at zoom.

30.text: tree, out of anger because her mother refused to take her along to the feast

32.text: This motive frequently plays a part even in cases of voluntary death

33.text: among old men, of which I shall speak later on. Thus in one of the texts

34.text: published in my “Chukchee Materials” (p. 52), a man, Little-Spoon, having

35.text: been angered by his sons, requested that he be killed. The Chukchee frequently

36.text: have a lurking inclination towards suicide, which is mentioned in the words

37.text: of Lotteri previously quoted, and is well known even to the Chukchee them-

38.text: selves. “You know our people,” I was told on several occasions. “For any

39.text: reason they want to kill another man or themselves.” During the epidemic
39.note: Machine text carried a stray escaped straight quote after 'themselves.'; print shows only the curly closing quote ” per keying_spec.md §1/§5.6.

40.text: of influenza on the Wolverine River, before mentioned, there occurred two

41.text: cases of suicide. One was that of a husband vexed at the loss of his young

42.text: wife; the other, that of a mother who had lost her only son, a child of ten.
